<description>
{
 "summary": "Counts accumulated chainwork during anti-DoS headers presync when checking outbound peers for chain sync eviction in `PeerManagerImpl::ConsiderEviction`. If the peer's accumulated presync work meets or exceeds the local node's tip work, the chain sync timeout is reset even though headers have not yet been stored in the block index. A new functional test reproduces the eviction timeout during slow presync and verifies that the peer remains connected.",
 "problem": "When a node's best header is below `-minimumchainwork`, incoming headers are held in presync and not stored in the block index, leaving `pindexBestKnownBlock` null for that peer. Chain sync eviction treats the peer as if it never announced a block and disconnects it after roughly 22 minutes (`CHAIN_SYNC_TIMEOUT` plus `HEADERS_RESPONSE_TIME`). On slow or high-latency links such as Tor or I2P, the ~480 round trips needed for mainnet presync can exceed 22 minutes, causing the node to repeatedly disconnect the sync peer and discard all presync progress.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description explains the interaction between #11490 (chain sync eviction) and #25717 (anti-DoS headers sync): 'The chain sync logic is from #11490, presync came later in #25717, and the two were never connected.'",
  "PR description notes mainnet impact: 'On mainnet presync is roughly 480 headers round trips. If that takes more than ~22 minutes (about 2.5 s per round trip, e.g. over slow Tor or I2P), the sync peer gets evicted before presync can finish, and the same thing can happen with the next peer.'",
  "The added functional test reproduces the bug: 'On master the peer is disconnected after 24 minutes. With the fix it stays connected and presynced_headers keeps going up.'"
 ],

<category name="p2p" title="P2P">
## Covers

Everything between this node and other nodes: connection management and
peer selection, address management, the message protocol and its
transport (including the encrypted v2 transport), block and transaction
relay including compact blocks, headers sync, transaction request and
orphan handling, network-level DoS protections, and the Tor, I2P, and
CJDNS integrations. The P2P and Private Broadcast labels are a strong
prior.

Not p2p: what the node does with a block or transaction once received
(validation, mempool); RPCs that merely report peer state (rpc).

## What matters here

Resistance to attack first: eclipse and partition resistance, DoS
resistance in message handling and resource accounting, and privacy of
transaction origin. Then relay correctness and liveness: blocks and
transactions propagate reliably and quickly, and nothing gets stuck.
Then interoperability with the rest of the network and with new
protocol features (BIPs) that other software depends on. Then bandwidth
and resource use, which node operators feel. Then connectivity across
network types and platforms.

Protocol changes with a specification and other implementations
waiting rank higher than local optimizations. Refactors count when they
retire a known hazard in message handling.
